name: Space and cosmic scale
purpose: big-idea explainers and scale comparisons, satellites as everyday infrastructure (navigation, timing, weather, communications), teamwork and procedures in high-stakes operations, technology and future topics

scenes.what: Earth seen from deep space with the 24 satellites of a satellite navigation constellation on their six tilted orbit rings around it, drawn at true scale, with the thin ring of low orbit hugging the planet and the far ring of geostationary orbit beyond
scenes.for: how satellite navigation (GPS) finds a position, why timing from space matters to networks and payments, how far away satellites really are, space as infrastructure (weather, communications), space debris and sustainability
plan: ABSTRACT (scale-free, no floor plan): a view of Earth from far out in space; the composition is set directly in frame terms and was not plan-checked.

Scale: Earth's radius (6,371 km) = 118 px, so 1 px is about 54 km. Everything that has a size here is at that scale: the navigation satellites orbit at about 20,200 km above the surface (a ring radius of about 26,560 km from Earth's centre = 492 px); the crewed station's low orbit at about 420 km up (a ring radius of 126 px, only 8 px above the surface); geostationary orbit at about 35,786 km up (a ring radius of 781 px).

The constellation (as the GPS baseline): 24 satellites, four on each of six orbit rings, each ring tilted 55 degrees to the equator and turned 60 degrees from the next around Earth's axis. The view looks at Earth from 18 degrees above the plane of its equator, so each ring shows as an ellipse.

Satellites are a few metres across, far too small to see at this scale: each is drawn as a small symbol about 14 px wide, which the scene says is not to scale. The rings' ellipses below were computed from this geometry.
scenes.camera: A distant view of Earth with no perspective (the planet and the rings are far smaller than the distance to them); Earth's centre at x 840, y 560; its north pole tipped 18 degrees toward the viewer, so the equator is a gentle curve below the centre.
scenes.composition: Earth is the focal shape: a disc 236 px across centred at x 840, y 560, the Sun lighting it from the right so the right two thirds are day and a soft terminator curves down its left third; the night side shows faint city lights. Its face is centred on the Atlantic: Africa and Europe on the lit right, the Americas at the left edge in the night side, white cloud bands and the blue ocean. Hugging it, the low orbit is a fine pale ring 8 px outside the surface (an ellipse 252 by 78 px). The six navigation rings form a cage of ellipses around it, all 984 px long (half-axis 492 px) and centred on Earth: ring 1 tilted 145 degrees counterclockwise from horizontal, half-width 457 px; ring 2 at 122 degrees, half-width 187; ring 3 at 142 degrees, half-width 184; ring 4 at 15 degrees, half-width 283; ring 5 at 52 degrees, seen almost edge on (half-width 14); ring 6 at 57 degrees, half-width 358. Together they span about x 359 to 1321 and y 91 to 1029. Where a ring passes behind Earth it is hidden by the disc. Satellites on the rings (as symbols): ring 1 at (1157, 229), (479, 227), (523, 891), (1201, 893); ring 2 at (668, 135), (593, 484), (1012, 985), (1087, 636); ring 3 at (583, 225), (1148, 610), (1097, 895), (532, 510); ring 4 at (994, 259), (1295, 573), (686, 861), (385, 547); ring 5 at (1140, 174), (540, 946), (866, 507), with its fourth hidden behind Earth at (814, 613); ring 6 at (702, 192), (464, 832), (978, 928), (1216, 288). Geostationary orbit is a faint dashed ellipse 1562 by 483 px in the equator's plane (x 59 to 1621, y 319 to 801), passing behind Earth. Background: black space with sparse, small, faint stars. Free zones for narrators, mascots and diagrams: (1) the upper right from x 1360 to 1880, y 60 to 300; (2) the lower right from x 1360 to 1880, y 830 to 1040; both clear of every ring.
scenes.light: The Sun is far off-frame to the right: Earth's day side is bright (blue ocean with a soft specular glint near its right limb, white clouds), a thin pale-blue atmosphere rim glows around the whole disc, brightest on the right; the terminator is soft; the night side is deep navy with warm pinpoint city lights. The satellite symbols are lit on their right faces (their solar panels glint). The rings are thin, light, semi-transparent lines (lm-light), the parts in front of Earth drawn over it, slightly brighter.
scenes.far: Black space with stars, the dashed geostationary ring's far half.
scenes.mid: Earth with its atmosphere rim, city lights and clouds; the low orbit ring; the six navigation rings and their satellites as separate groups (ring_1 to ring_6), each split into the part behind Earth and the part in front.
scenes.near: Nothing in front: the free zones stay open.

scenes.what: the Sun and the eight planets side by side at their true relative sizes, from the edge of the Sun's huge disc on the left to Neptune on the right, with Earth's Moon beside Earth; the distances between them are not to scale
scenes.for: scale comparisons and big numbers made concrete, putting a change or a risk in proportion, the size of the opportunity, curiosity openers for science and technology topics
plan: ABSTRACT (scale-free, no floor plan): a lineup diagram in space; the composition is set directly in frame terms and was not plan-checked.

Sizes are true to one scale: 1 px = 447 km. Diameters: the Sun 3,116 px (so only the edge of its disc fits), Mercury 11 px, Venus 27, Earth 29, the Moon 8, Mars 15, Jupiter 320, Saturn 270 (its main rings 610 px across), Uranus 114, Neptune 111 (from the NASA planetary fact sheet).
Distances are NOT to scale: at this scale Neptune would be about 10 million px from the Sun. The planets stand in their order from the Sun, evenly spaced; the scene says so in its note slot.
scenes.camera: A flat, side-on lineup with no perspective: every centre on one level line at y 600.
scenes.composition: The Sun's edge fills the left edge: a huge curved limb whose centre is far off-frame left, its edge at x 200 on the centre line, x 171 at y 300 and y 900, and x 103 at the top and bottom of the frame. Then, centres on y 600 from left to right: Mercury (11 px) at x 240; Venus (27 px) at x 282; Earth (29 px) at x 330 with the Moon (8 px) just above right of it at x 360, y 585; Mars (15 px) at x 385; Jupiter (320 px) at x 590, spanning x 430 to 750; Saturn (body 270 px) at x 1095 with its rings tipped open about 20 degrees, an ellipse 610 by about 210 px (x 790 to 1400); Uranus (114 px) at x 1530; Neptune (111 px) at x 1720. The four small inner planets sit close to the Sun's edge as a tight group of dots; the jump to Jupiter is the focal surprise. Background: black space with sparse, faint stars. Free zones for narrators, mascots and labels: (1) the band above the lineup from x 260 to 1880, y 60 to 400; (2) the band below it from x 260 to 1880, y 800 to 1040; neither is crossed by a planet or the rings.
scenes.light: The Sun is the only light, on the left: its disc a white-yellow with a slightly darker, orange-tinted limb, fine granulation and two small dark sunspots near its edge, a soft glow spilling a little into space. Every planet is lit from the left with a soft terminator about a third of the way in from its right edge, the right side falling into deep shade. Colours are the real ones: Mercury dark grey with craters; Venus pale yellow-white cloud; Earth blue with white cloud and a hint of land; the Moon grey; Mars rusty orange-red with a white polar cap; Jupiter cream and tan bands with the reddish Great Red Spot in its southern half; Saturn pale gold with faint bands, its rings cream with a dark gap (the Cassini division) and casting a thin shadow on the planet; Uranus pale cyan and almost featureless; Neptune deep blue with faint bands. Faint rings of Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune are not drawn.
scenes.far: Black space with its stars, and the Sun's limb with its glow.
scenes.mid: Each planet as its own group (mercury, venus, earth, moon, mars, jupiter, saturn with saturn_rings, uranus, neptune), so each can be pointed at or moved.
scenes.near: Nothing in front: the free zones stay open.

scenes.what: inside a laboratory module of a crewed space station in low Earth orbit, looking along its square aisle of equipment racks to the open hatch at the far end, with a round window in the deck showing Earth
scenes.for: checklists and procedures, teamwork in a small crew, working in isolation and remote teams, planning and routines, handling a malfunction calmly, wellbeing under pressure
plan: Metres: x to the right (starboard), y away from the camera (forward, along the module), z up from the deck (the side the crew treat as the floor). There is no gravity: up and down are a crew convention, kept here so the set reads.

The module is a cylinder about 8.5 m long and 4.3 m across outside; inside, racks line all four sides and leave a square aisle about 2.1 m wide and 2.1 m high: port rack faces at x -1.05, starboard at x 1.05, deck at z 0, overhead at z 2.1, from the aft hatch (behind the camera, y 0) to the forward bulkhead at y 7.8.

Racks: each about 1.05 m wide, side by side along each wall with their joints at y 1.2, 2.25, 3.3, 4.35, 5.4, 6.45 and 7.5. Near racks carry equipment (panels, a glovebox, laptops on arms, cable bundles); the three racks on each side from y 4.35 to 7.5 are stowage racks closed with plain white fabric closeouts.
The forward bulkhead (y 7.8) has an open square hatch 1.27 m wide (x -0.63 to 0.63, z 0.45 to 1.72) into a brightly lit node beyond.

A round window 0.5 m across is set in the deck at (0, 4.6), showing Earth below. LED light panels run along the four corners where the walls meet the overhead and the deck. Handrails along every wall at about z 1.1; foot loops on the deck.
Cast: A stands with feet in the deck's foot loops at (-0.45, 3.0); B at (0.7, 3.6), also in foot loops, turned to A. Both upright by the crew's convention.

Camera: x 0.2, y 0 at the aft hatch, eye 1.65 m above the deck (floating slightly high), looking straight forward along the aisle; a wide lens (about 75 degrees across, the width a real interior camera uses in a module this small); no tilt; horizon at 50 percent.
scenes.camera: A floating camera at the aft end of the module, eye 1.65 m above the deck, looking straight down the aisle; wide lens, about 75 degrees across; no tilt. One-point perspective: the vanishing point at x 960, y 540; the racks' joints, the light panels, the handrails and the deck's lines all run to it.
scenes.composition: A square tunnel of racks recedes to the far bulkhead, a smaller square framed from x 760 to 1096 and y 468 to 805, with the open hatch in it (x 827 to 1029, y 529 to 732) glowing with the brighter light of the node beyond. The near racks rise out of the frame on both sides, the overhead out of the top and the deck out of the bottom; the rack joints step in toward the centre (on the port wall at x 600, 670, 718 and 751 for the joints at 4.35, 5.4, 6.45 and 7.5 m; on the starboard wall at x 1204, 1157, 1125 and 1102). The light panels are bright lines along the overhead corners (from about x 209 and 1460 at y 290 near the camera to x 746 and 1103 at y 469 far away). The round deck window sits low in the centre, seen at a low angle as a flattened oval (x 838 to 974, y about 966 to 1015, centre y 989), Earth's surface in it: blue ocean and white cloud seen from straight above. A laptop on an arm at the starboard wall (x 1377, y 722), a handrail along the port wall (x 531, y 737 at 3.5 m). Focal point: the lit hatch at the far end. Free zones for the cast: (1) A on the left, seen from the knees up (head top x 689, y 498; head centre y 548), the head against the plain white closeouts of the port wall's far stowage racks; (2) B on the right, turned toward A, seen from the knees up (head top x 1134, y 505; head centre y 547), the head against the white closeouts of the starboard wall's far stowage racks. Their feet are below the frame.
scenes.light: Even, cool-white light from the LED panels along the four corners, bright and nearly shadowless, with small soft shadows under handrails and cable bundles; the white closeouts and panels glow softly; the far node is a little brighter and warmer, so the hatch reads as a lit opening. Earth in the deck window is sunlit, blue ocean with white cloud, giving a faint blue spill on the deck around it.
scenes.far: The far bulkhead with the hatch and the node beyond, the stowage racks and their white closeouts, the overhead and deck racks, the light panels, the deck window with Earth, and the near racks' equipment along both walls.
scenes.mid: The laptop on its arm, a tethered pen floating beside it, and a drink pouch stuck to a wall patch.
scenes.near: The edges of the nearest racks at the frame's left and right edges and a cable bundle crossing the top left corner (about x 0 to 260, y 0 to 120), cropped by the frame; they touch no cast zone.

aliases: control room for a space mission
scenes.what: the space programme's flight control room seen from its back row: four long rows of consoles facing a front wall of three large screens, the room dim so the screens and the consoles' monitors glow
scenes.for: incident response and crisis management (work the problem), clear roles and communication under pressure, decision-making with data, handovers between shifts, teamwork across specialists
plan: Metres: x to the right, y away from the camera (toward the front wall), z up from the floor. The room is 20 m wide (x 0 to 20) and 16 m deep (back wall at y 0, behind the camera; front wall at y 16), with a flat floor and a dark acoustic ceiling at 6.0 m.

The front wall carries three large screens side by side, each 5.2 m wide and 2.6 m tall with its bottom edge 2.6 m above the floor (so seated controllers see them over their monitors): centred at x 4.5, 10 and 15.5. Above them a strip of time displays (slots) at about 5.5 m. Below them plain dark acoustic wall panels.

Four rows of consoles run across the room, each a long desk 0.8 m deep and 0.75 m high from x 3 to 17, with two or three monitors per position (tops at 1.25 m) on its far edge, all facing the front wall, chairs on the camera side: row 1 (front) at y 12.5, row 2 at y 9.5, row 3 at y 6.5 (the flight director's position in its middle, at x 10), row 4 (back) at y 3.5.
Cast: A and B stand in the aisle between row 4 and row 3, A at (7.2, 5.3) and B at (9.4, 4.9), facing each other or the screens; the back row's desk and monitors stand between them and the camera.
Camera: x 7.5, y 0.4 (just inside the back wall), eye 1.6 m, turned 8 degrees right of straight ahead; about 60 degrees across; no tilt; horizon at 46 percent.
scenes.camera: A standing camera at the back of the room behind the last row of consoles, eye 1.6 m, turned 8 degrees right; about 60 degrees across; no tilt. Horizon at y 497 (46 percent). The rows and the front wall run across the frame almost level (their vanishing point is far off-frame right, x about 12790); lines running toward the front wall meet at x 726 on the horizon.
scenes.composition: The three big screens fill the top of the frame along the front wall: left x 85 to 683 (y 108 to 383), centre x 715 to 1256 (y 126 to 389), right x 1286 to 1778 (y 143 to 394), each glowing with an abstract display (slots); the time-display strip above them (x 334 to 1584, y about 69 to 82). Below the screens, a calm band of dark wall panels runs across the frame from about y 390 down to the far consoles. The four rows of consoles step toward the camera: the front row's monitor backs at about y 541 to 547, row 2's at about y 555 to 564, row 3's at about y 588 to 599 (the flight director's position at x 1383, y 588), and the back row nearest, its desk's front edge crossing the lower frame from x 37, y 884 to x 2078, y 822 with its monitors' backs standing on it (tops about y 660 to 700). Empty chairs stand at each position on the camera side. Focal point: the centre screen. Free zones for the cast, both seen from the hips up over the back row's monitors: (1) A left of centre (head top x 622, y 445; head centre y 486), the head against the dark wall panels below the left screen, about 60 px under its bottom edge; (2) B right of centre (head top x 1402, y 444; head centre y 486), against the panels below the right screen, about 50 px under it. Their feet stand on the floor behind the back row, about y 1050 to 1060.
scenes.light: The room is kept dim: the three screens are the brightest things, their cool glow lighting the front of the room and the tops of the consoles; small downlights in the dark ceiling make soft pools on the desks; the monitors' backs are dark, with a faint rim of light from their screens; the aisle between rows is in soft half-light. A low warm wash along the back row's desk from a desk lamp. No daylight, no windows.
scenes.far: The front wall with its screens and the time strip, the dark panels below them, the ceiling, the side walls, and consoles rows 1 to 3 with their chairs, drawn complete across the room, and the floor of the aisle where the cast stand.
scenes.mid: The back row: its long desk, its monitors (backs toward the camera), headsets and papers on it; it stands in front of the cast's lower bodies.
scenes.near: Two empty chairs of the back row, their backs toward the camera, cropped by the bottom edge at the left and right (about x 0 to 300 and x 1600 to 1920, below y 860); they touch no cast zone.

core: planets set (true colours and relative sizes)

identity.place: Earth's neighbourhood as one fictional international crewed space programme of the early 2030s sees it: the programme's flight control room on the ground, its laboratory module on a crewed station in low Earth orbit about 420 km up, the satellites that circle Earth (a satellite navigation constellation about 20,200 km up), and the Sun and planets around them. No real agency, mission, spacecraft or logo is drawn; Earth, the Moon, the Sun and the planets are the real ones, at their real sizes and colours whenever a scene states them.
architecture: space itself: black, with sparse, small, faint stars (bright stars are few; a sunlit scene washes most of them out); no nebula clouds or coloured gas near Earth

Earth from space: deep blue oceans, white cloud bands and spirals, brown and green land, a thin pale-blue line of atmosphere at the limb, city lights on the night side; a soft terminator between day and night

satellites: small boxy bodies with two flat solar panel wings and a few antennas, a few metres across; navigation satellites circle about 20,200 km up on six rings tilted 55 degrees to the equator, four or more per ring

the station module: a cylinder about 8.5 m long and 4.3 m across whose inside is lined on all four sides with equipment racks about 1.05 m wide, leaving a square aisle about 2.1 m high and wide; square hatches about 1.27 m at each end; handrails, foot loops, fastening patches, cable bundles and LED light panels along the corners

the flight control room: a large, dim, flat-floored room about 20 by 16 m with four long rows of consoles (desks with two or three monitors per position, headsets, binders) facing a front wall of large screens set high enough to see over the monitors; dark acoustic walls and ceiling with small downlights
the Sun and planets: the real bodies at their real relative sizes and colours (NASA planetary fact sheet)
identity.materials: in space: black sky, white and blue Earth, grey and gold satellites with dark-blue solar panels; in the station: off-white rack faces and fabric closeouts, grey fastening patches, aluminium handrails, black cable bundles, laptop screens; in the control room: dark grey acoustic panels, charcoal consoles with dark monitor backs, glowing screens. Palette families in this world (the set palette was named for rooms): the black of space is sky (its deep tone) and the station's and room's main surfaces are wall; screens that are off and monitor backs are screen; lit screens are paper hi with slots; Earth's oceans are glass, its land plant, its clouds paper; satellites and handrails are metal, their solar panels glass; the planets use the families nearest their real colours (Mars and Jupiter's spot brick, Saturn and Venus paper or brass, Uranus and Neptune glass); the Sun is light; warning lights are accent
inhabited: the station is lived in: a tethered pen, a drink pouch stuck to a wall patch, a checklist clipped to a handrail, cargo bags strapped in place
the control room is worked in: headsets left on monitors, an open procedures binder, a coffee cup, a jacket on a chair
space is busy: satellites on their rings, the station's thin low orbit, the geostationary ring far out
nothing floats loose in the station unless it is shown drifting on purpose
scale: Earth's radius is 6,371 km; the crewed station flies about 420 km up (1.07 Earth radii from the centre); navigation satellites about 20,200 km up (4.17 Earth radii from the centre); geostationary satellites about 35,786 km up (6.6 Earth radii)
the Moon is 3,475 km across, about a quarter of Earth, and about 384,400 km away (60 Earth radii)

planet diameters: Mercury 4,879 km, Venus 12,104, Earth 12,756, Mars 6,792, Jupiter 142,984, Saturn 120,536 (its main rings about 273,000 km across), Uranus 51,118, Neptune 49,528; the Sun 1,392,700 km (about 109 Earths)
a person is about 1.75 m tall; the station's aisle is about 2.1 m square; a hatch about 1.27 m square; a station rack about 1.05 m wide
a control room console desk is 0.75 m high with monitors to about 1.25 m; the front screens about 5.2 by 2.6 m, their bottoms 2.6 m above the floor
identity.default_light: In space: hard, white sunlight from one side and black shadow on the other, with no air to soften it; Earth's day side bright and its night side dark with city lights. Inside the station: even, cool-white LED light from the panels along the corners. In the control room: dim, focused light from small downlights, with the screens glowing.
identity.motifs: Use at least three of these in every scene so the sets belong to one programme (each scene names the ones its camera can see): Earth from space with its thin blue atmosphere, satellites on their orbits, the station's white racks and handrails, the big screens with an orbit track and Earth (as abstract slots), rows of consoles with headsets, a floating loose object, the planets in their true colours, the Sun's edge, the dim, focused light of a control room, Earth seen from orbit (through a window), the empty space where a scale note goes.
avoid: real agency logos, flags, mission patches, spacecraft names or real spacecraft drawn recognisably
sci-fi: glowing corridors, holograms, laser beams, spaceships with fins
planets or orbits at the wrong sizes when a scene says it is to scale
sound waves, flames or smoke in space
people in the sets (the cast is separate)
identity.outside: Seen from the station's window: Earth's curve, cloud and ocean; from the control room: nothing (it has no windows).

objects.Earth: the real Earth seen from space: a sphere with deep blue oceans, white cloud bands and spirals, brown and green continents, polar ice, a thin pale-blue glowing line of atmosphere around its edge; lit on one side by the Sun with a soft terminator; city lights as warm pinpoints on the night side
objects.orbit rings: thin, light, semi-transparent lines tracing circular orbits around Earth, drawn as ellipses because they are tilted to the view; the part behind Earth hidden by the planet
objects.navigation satellite: a satellite navigation spacecraft drawn as a small symbol (about 14 px): a boxy body with two flat dark-blue solar panel wings on a short boom, a flat antenna panel facing Earth; no markings
objects.low orbit ring: the low orbit where the crewed station flies, about 420 km above the surface: a fine pale ring just outside Earth's edge
objects.geostationary ring: the ring of geostationary orbit about 35,786 km above the equator, in the equator's plane: a faint dashed ellipse
objects.the Moon: the real Moon: a grey sphere with darker grey seas (maria) and a few bright craters, about a quarter of Earth's width; lit from the same side as Earth
objects.star field: black space with sparse, small, faint white stars of slightly different sizes, a few slightly warmer or bluer; no nebulae
objects.the Sun: the real Sun: a white-yellow disc with a slightly darker, orange-tinted limb (limb darkening), fine granulation texture, a few small dark sunspots with paler edges, and a soft glow around it
objects.Mercury: a small dark-grey rocky planet covered in craters
objects.Venus: a planet wrapped in smooth, pale yellow-white cloud with faint bands, no surface visible
objects.Mars: a rusty orange-red planet with darker grey-brown regions and a small white polar ice cap
objects.Jupiter: a giant planet with cream, tan and brown horizontal cloud bands and swirls, and the oval reddish Great Red Spot in its southern half
objects.Saturn: a pale gold planet with faint horizontal bands, circled by broad flat cream rings with a dark gap (the Cassini division), tilted so the rings show as a wide ellipse and cast a thin shadow on the planet
objects.Uranus: a pale cyan, almost featureless planet
objects.Neptune: a deep blue planet with faint lighter bands and a small dark spot
objects.station rack: an equipment rack about 1.05 m wide filling the wall from deck to overhead: off-white face panels with rows of small fasteners, some with built-in equipment (a glovebox window, small control panels with switches and blank displays), cable bundles along its edges
objects.fabric closeout: a plain off-white fabric cover stretched over the front of a stowage rack, with faint seams and a few zip pulls; calm and plain
objects.hatch: a square hatch opening about 1.27 m wide with rounded corners and a thick metal rim, its hinged hatch door folded back out of the way; the brightly lit node beyond
objects.deck window: a round window about 0.5 m across set in a thick ring frame in the deck, with Earth's surface seen below through it
objects.light panel: long flat LED light panels along the corners where the walls meet the overhead and the deck, glowing cool white
objects.handrail: a short aluminium handrail about 0.5 m long fixed to the rack faces on two stand-off feet, at about 1.1 m above the deck; many of them along the walls
objects.foot loops: soft fabric loops fixed to the deck where the crew slip their feet in to hold themselves in place
objects.laptop on an arm: a laptop held open on an adjustable metal arm fixed to a rack, its screen a slot
objects.big screen: a large flat display about 5.2 by 2.6 m set into the front wall in a thin dark frame, glowing with an abstract display (a slot)
objects.console row: a long control-room desk 0.8 m deep and 0.75 m high in charcoal grey, divided into positions about 1.6 m wide, each with two or three monitors on the far edge, a keyboard, a headset and a phone panel
objects.console monitor: a flat monitor on a stand, seen from behind as a dark rectangle with a faint rim of light from its screen
objects.control room chair: an office task chair with a black mesh back, armrests and a five-castor base
objects.headset: a single-ear headset with a boom microphone and a coiled cable, hanging on a monitor's corner
objects.time display strip: a row of rectangular time displays in a thin dark frame above the big screens (slots, no digits drawn)
objects.acoustic wall panel: dark grey fabric-faced acoustic panels covering the walls in large plain rectangles with thin joints

research: Space facts checked on 2026-10-15 (the GPS constellation's altitude, planes and inclination; planet and Sun diameters; the station laboratory module's size, racks and window; flight control room layouts). Sources and what was not verified: docs/research/2026-10-13-sets-space.md.
